title: Async vs Sync — How FastAPI Runs Your Code
summary: Learn when to use async def vs def, and avoid the #1 FastAPI performance bug.

sections.content: FastAPI runs on an ASGI event loop. The key distinction is between async def and def route operations:

items: async def → runs ON the event loop (single thread, many concurrent requests)
def → runs in a THREADPOOL (anyio, default 40 threads)

rows: Never mix sync calls in async def

sections.title: #1 FastAPI Performance Bug
sections.content: Calling blocking sync code (requests.get(), time.sleep(), psycopg2) inside an async def route blocks the ENTIRE event loop. No other request can be served until it finishes. This kills concurrency.
Example: The Right and Wrong Way
When to Use a Task Queue Instead
For truly long-running or CPU-heavy work (ML inference, report generation, ETL), don't do it in the request path at all. Use a task queue (Celery, arq, taskiq, RQ) with workers scaled independently.

quiz.question: What happens if you call time.sleep(5) inside an async def route?
options: It blocks the entire event loop for 5 seconds
quiz.explanation: Blocking calls inside async def block the event loop. No other request can be served during those 5 seconds. This is the #1 FastAPI performance bug.

quiz.question: Where does a def (sync) route operation run?
quiz.explanation: def routes run in anyio's threadpool, so blocking calls there don't affect the event loop. The event loop can still serve other requests.

quiz.question: Which HTTP client should you use in an async def route?
quiz.explanation: Use async libraries like httpx.AsyncClient in async routes. Using sync requests blocks the event loop.

quiz.question: What should you do for CPU-heavy work (image processing, ML inference)?
options: Use def (threadpool) or a task queue
quiz.explanation: CPU-heavy work blocks regardless of async/sync. Use def (threadpool) for short tasks, or a task queue (Celery, arq) for long-running work.

quiz.question: How many threads does the default anyio threadpool have?
quiz.explanation: The default anyio threadpool has 40 threads. This limits how many concurrent sync (def) routes can run simultaneously.
